newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais privatisation could be accelerated.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais privatisation could be accelerated.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, whose centre-right coalition is fighting for re-election, said on Thursday the government could speed up plans to privatise the Credit Lyonnais bank and sell it this year.

Attacking the proposal of the opposition Socialists to put privatisation on hold, he told the business daily Les Echos the bank and other state-owned firms had to be sold to avert "disasters like Credit Lyonnais," whose cost to taxpayers is likely to exceed 100 billion francs ($17.5 billion).
The bank almost collapsed in the early 1990s under the weight of lending excesses but has since staged a strong rebound, helped by massive doses of state aid.

On Thursday, it said first-quarter pre-tax, pre-exceptional profit was up significantly from the same period in 1996 but gave no precise figures. Credit Lyonnais shares finished 2.55 percent higher at 221.50 francs against an overall weaker market.

Juppe's comment that Credit Lyonnais could be on the market this year, instead of late in 1998 or early 1999 as planned, followed allegations by a state-backed company that the bank had been a victim of a "veritable looting" before 1993.

The claims by the Consortium de Realisation (CDR), set up in 1995 to liquidate nearly 200 million francs of the bank's dud assets, stoked an already intense election debate over the need to privatise state firms.

The centre-right governing coalition has been seeking during the election campaign to make political capital out of the Socialists' disastrous record of managing state companies while they were in power.
The first round of voting will be held on May 25 with the final round on June 1.

The CDR said in a staff newsletter given to Reuters its audit teams had uncovered the existence of a massive organised financial fraud in seven of Credit Lyonnais' subsidiaries which have since been hived off to clean up the bank's balance sheet.
The fraud, it said, had been concealed by false balance sheets and facilitated by "obliging management."

The cost of "this financial apocalypse" was above figures recently mentioned, it said. CDR chairman Michel Rouger told a parliamentary commission earlier this year that bank executives had swindled five billion francs before 1993. But Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade in March called the sum a fabrication.

The newsletter was intended as a "morale-boosting exercise for the troops in face of attacks from various quarters" over the CDR's performance in selling off the bank's assets, a CDR spokesman said, without specifying the origin of the attacks.
He said Rouger had made similar comments to the parliamentary committee investigating the banking scandal.

Some 75 legal proceedings are underway involving the affair, with more expected. Last year, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said he wanted to bring former senior bank managers to justice for failing to keep control of the subsidiaries during the expansion spree.
Separately, Credit Lyonnais stressed that the allegations made by the CDR involved the "old Credit Lyonnais" and that the subsidiaries involved no longer belonged to the bank.

"People must distinguish between the Credit Lyonnais of today, which is on the road to recovery, and the Credit Lyonnais of the past. These problems involve (Credit Lyonnais) subsidiaries before 1993," said a spokesman for the bank.

Banking analysts said it was unlikely the bank could be sold this year in light of expected disposals the bank would have to make to win European Commission approval for the state aid needed to make it ready for sale.
Some media reports say the bank could need a further eight to 12 billion franc injection to boost its solvency ratios.
The government had said the bank would receive no further public money before privatisation but recently suggested some funds could be available when it is privatised.
Analysts said the bank could be ready for sale in early 1998. "Many investors would prefer a full year of solid operating performance, rather than half a year," said one.
"I see it as viable for sale in the first half of 1998 either as a public offering or for sale to another bank," said Salomon Brothers analyst John Leonard. ($ = 5.712 French Francs)
